title: People Do Not Do What You Say. They Do What You Reward
author: Lead With Kelly
summary: The author recounts a career-defining moment as a young executive when a factory floor site leader told him plainly, in front of his team, that 'the company did not care about cash' -- a statement the author eventually recognized as an accurate reading of five years of behavior, not a complaint. Despite genuinely caring about cash and saying so in meetings, the author's organization consistently rewarded and gave attention to quarterly earnings, and the monthly cash report was reliably skipped -- a signal, he argues, that was read perfectly and transmitted intact down every level of the hierarchy to the factory floor. When the business eventually generated negative cash flow, the resulting fix compounded the same underlying disease: because changing years of behavior takes years, the organization resorted to short-term moves that pulled cash forward at the expense of long-term value, essentially repeating the same 'optimize one number' pattern with a different number. The turnaround only came when the leadership team changed what it visibly, consistently paid attention to, leading to the article's core claim: people learn what an organization actually values not from its stated words but from what it spends time and rewards on, and leaders are 'always teaching,' whether they intend to or not.
points: Uses a single factory-floor exchange -- a site leader stating flatly that 'the company did not care about cash' -- as proof that organizational signals are read accurately and transmitted intact through every level of a hierarchy, regardless of what leadership says in meetings.

Identifies a specific, replicable diagnostic: what gets consistently skipped in a recurring report or meeting agenda is a more honest signal of organizational priorities than anything printed in a mission statement.

Notes the 'cruel' irony that the initial fix for the resulting cash crisis repeated the same underlying disease -- sacrificing long-term value for short-term optimization of a single number, just a different number than before.

Concludes that fixing the culture required no speech, only changing where leadership's visible attention went -- moving the ignored report to the top of every meeting until the organization believed, through observed behavior, that it actually mattered.
quotes: He did not say it as a complaint. He said it as a fact, the way you tell a visitor which way is north. And the thing that has stayed with me for twenty years is that he was right.
I cared about cash. I pushed it, raised it in meetings, argued it mattered. But I could see what actually got rewarded, and it was earnings. So I chased it.
The words said cash mattered. The attention said it did not. So did the money, since the incentives all paid out on earnings. And the organization was never confused about which signal to believe.
You cannot spend five years signaling that something does not matter and then act surprised when no one has been tending it.
It changed when the attention changed. The cash page stopped getting skipped. It moved up in the deck, ahead of earnings, so it was the first thing we looked at instead of the last thing we ignored.
